claims.text: CrCoNi exhibits non-random chemical short-range ordering.
CrCoNi contains L12-type short-range order that minimizes Cr–Cr nearest-neighbor interactions.
The degree and type of short-range chemical order govern toughness retention in CrCoNi.
Heat treatment can shift CrCoNi from predominantly L11 short-range order toward increased L12 short-range order.
A homogenized CrCoNi sample predominantly exhibits L11-type short-range order.
Both L11- and L12-type short-range order occur within nanoclusters in CrCoNi.
Changing the local chemical ordering alters dislocation-slip behavior.
L12-type ordering produces more ductile dislocation-slip behavior than L11-type ordering.
L12 ordering may activate more favorable slip systems or reduce stress concentrations at dislocation pile-ups.
L11 ordering is associated with a less favorable dislocation response leading to brittleness.
Heat-treatment-promoted L12 formation is accompanied by a dramatic change in dislocation-slip behavior.
Increasing L12 ordering will improve fracture toughness relative to the homogenized L11-dominant baseline.
The homogenized L11-dominant baseline has lower toughness and less favorable slip behavior.
Electron nanodiffraction, neutron scattering, and atom probe tomography can be used to characterize short-range ordering in CrCoNi.
The proposed behavior should hold from ambient to moderate temperatures where short-range order remains stable and diffusion permits ordering changes without large-scale phase separation.
The hypothesis likely extends to similar non-dilute concentrated alloys when short-range order dominates dislocation dynamics.
The hypothesis may not apply when long-range ordering or severe phase separation dominates the microstructure.
Similar toughness despite demonstrably different L11/L12 ordering would falsify the proposed ordering-controlled toughness relationship.
